alternative_names: Charlotte Smith, of Bignor Park, in Sussex
birthplace: London, King Street, off St James's Square, born on 4 May 1749, the eldest daughter of Nicholas Turner of Stoke House, Surrey, and Anna (Towers) Turner
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the pre-Romantic and Romantic lyric tradition of the sensibility and the sonnet revival, joined to the radical and domestic novel of the 1790s and to the educational literature for young women produced by the London and provincial presses between the French Revolution and her death
literary_identity: Poet and novelist who revived the regular English sonnet in the 1780s and, from 1789 to 1806, supported herself by her pen through a series of epistolary and domestic novels, juvenile letters, a blank-verse poem on the French Revolution and a topographical poem of the Sussex coast
biography: Charlotte Turner was born in King Street, off St James's Square, London, on 4 May 1749, the eldest daughter of Nicholas Turner of Stoke House, Surrey, a country gentleman, and Anna Turner. Her mother died early and, after her father's reckless speculation dissolved the family fortune, she was largely raised by an aunt and put to girls' schools at Chichester. On 23 February 1765, aged fifteen, she was given by her father in marriage to Benjamin Smith, a much older man of violent temper and ruinous debts whom she afterwards described as a species of sale; the marriage produced a large family, twelve children being counted, of whom six survived her. The couple lived successively on the Isle of Wight and in Hampshire and Sussex, and Smith filled her years of marriage with the duties of a gentleman's wife, French and Italian reading, drawing, music and the care of her children's education. Benjamin Smith squandered a considerable legacy and was committed to the King's Bench prison for debt in December 1783, where his wife stayed with him, and it was during these years of confinement and disgrace that she assembled Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems (1784), the little volume which made her name and went through nine or more enlarged editions in her lifetime. On her separation from her husband she became, in effect, the first English woman of letters to live by professional authorship under the modern meaning of the word: she wrote a novel, a juvenile work or a volume of verse almost annually for the rest of her life, and her later title pages describe her as 'Charlotte Smith, of Bignor Park, in Sussex'. From 1776 the disposition of a family inheritance worth nearly £36,000, settled on her by her uncle James Turner in preference to her brother George, was tied up in Chancery for almost forty years; the litigation, its costs and the failures of her solicitors absorbed her income and her attention until her death and long afterwards, and she dedicated much of her preface-writing to telling the story of it. She lived in consequence at Chichester, Brighton, Storrington, Bath, Exmouth, Weymouth, Oxford, London, Frant and Elstead, moving whenever her creditors or her health required it; at Brighton in 1791-3 she was in the company of English radicals, and her sympathy with the Revolution in France, openly declared in Desmond (1792) and The Banished Man (1794), cost her subscribers and publishers in the reaction of the late 1790s. She corresponded with Joseph Cooper Walker, with the Cadells and with Samuel Harper, and in her last years her health failed, one eye being lost and her chest disease advancing. Charlotte Smith died at Tilford in Surrey on 28 October 1806 and was buried at Stoke Church, Stoke Park, near Guildford, within sight of the downs she had celebrated; she was widely lamented, especially by other women writers, and left unfinished manuscripts which her daughter published afterwards.
literary_profile: Her poetry begins with Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems (London, 1784), enlarged in successive editions (third edition 1786; fifth 1789; seventh 1795; eighth 1797; ninth 1800) by new sonnets, by translations and imitations from Petrarch and other originals, and by an increasingly explicit advertisement of the poet's own injuries. To it she appended the two-book blank-verse poem The Emigrants (1793), on the French royalist exiles of the Revolution, and her last and most assured volume, Beachy Head, and Other Poems (1807), published after her death and including shorter pieces such as 'Flora' and 'Studies by the Sea' which had first appeared in her juvenile books. Her fiction, when she resumed it after 1788, is at the centre of her modern reputation: Ethelinde, or, The Recluse of the Lake (1789), Celestina (1791), Desmond (1792), The Old Manor House (1793), The Wanderings of Warwick (1794), The Banished Man (1794), Montalbert (1795), Marchmont (1796) and The Young Philosopher (1798), with the tale-series The Letters of a Solitary Wanderer (1800). She also made a permanent parallel reputation as an educational writer, in The Rural Walks (1795), Rambles Farther (1796), Minor Morals (1798) and Conversations, Introducing Poetry to the Young (1804), and she printed A Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports (1796) for the benefit of a survivor of the wreck. Her earlier books, the translation The Romance of Real Life (1787) and the revised edition of her first novel Emmeline (Cadell, 1788), belong to the eighteenth century; the collections and the comedy got up after 1806, including the Commonplace Book and the novel attributed to her as the Literary Don Quixote, extend the record but not the lifetime's work. Modern scholarship is served by Stuart Curran's edition of her Poems (Oxford University Press, 1993), by Judith Phillips Stanton's Collected Letters (Indiana University Press, 2003), by the Pickering and Chatto collected edition of her Works in a numbered series of volumes, and by the essay collection Charlotte Smith in British Romanticism edited by Jacqueline Labbe (2008).
stylistic_characteristics: Her sonnets are written in the regular fourteen-line form she preferred, with an attention to turn and closure that she set against what she thought the license of the Pindaric and Della Cruscan modes; the diction is that of sensibility - elegiac, personal, topographically exact, frequently addressed to a river, a headland, an old tree or a remembered haunt, and closing on a pointed couplet or a turned sentence. She introduced into the lyric a documentary force, the poet's own history of injury and dependence appearing in prefatory prose beside the verses. Her novels are mostly epistolary and self-consciously empirical, opening with an advertisement or prefatory letter claiming that the events are drawn from real life and from her own observation, and dividing sympathy between an impoverished heroine, a disputed heir and an oppressive relative; Gothic machinery - the abbey, the castle, the secret of birth - is retained but explained by law, money and interest rather than by fate. The juvenile books put instruction into conversation and the familiar letter, with natural-history observation and short quoted poems as the method of teaching. Her late blank verse, in The Emigrants and Beachy Head, is descriptive and meditative, moving from panoramic landscape to local history and personal resignation in the same sentence.
intellectual_concerns: The condition of a woman compelled to make a living by writing, and the dependence, debt and litigation that governed her work; the justice of property, the rights of an disinherited heir and the operation of law and the equity courts upon families; the French Revolution followed at first hand and in its effects on exiles, on the poor and on the conscience of a sympathiser; the education of young women and the uses of conversation, natural history and poetry as teaching; the claims of sensibility and their limits; landscape as evidence of feeling and as a record of loss; the superstition and the suffering of Catholic and rural communities; and the dignity of the humble and the aged, especially women, in a poetry of place.
historical_significance: By reviving the legitimate sonnet in the 1780s and holding it open through nine editions she made the form available for the meditative and personal use that Wordsworth and his contemporaries afterwards made standard; Stuart Curran's judgement that she is 'the first poet in English whom in retrospect we would call Romantic' states the modern claim. Her novels supplied the model of empirical, socially realistic domestic fiction written by a woman for a professional living, and Desmond and The Old Manor House are now read as political fictions of the 1790s answering Godwin and arguing with the reaction; her juvenile books carried that realism into the education of girls. Her long Chancery suit and her prefaces made the economics of authorship part of her texts, and her recovery since the 1990s, through Curran's, Stanton's and the Pickering and Chatto editions, has made her the central case in scholarship on women's writing, the sonnet revival and Romantic print culture.
biographical_uncertainty: Her birth is fixed at 4 May 1749 by the Dictionary of National Biography tradition and by modern accounts, but older reference works long hesitated over the year, and her own statements about her childhood differ; the day and year of several first editions remain disputed in the secondary literature, Desmond (1792 in the English Short Title Catalogue records inspected here) still often being cited as 1796, and the revised Emmeline as 1788 or 1789 according to the copy examined; the attribution of the anonymous comedy What Is She? (printed 1799) is accepted by some modern scholars and doubted by others; the number of her children and the details of her residence at Bignor Park are variously reported; and the date at which her Chancery suit ceased to be pending is usually given from her own letters rather than from the court records.

birthplace: Bristol, daughter of Nicholas Darby, a captain in the navy who deserted his family; the register of St Augustine's Church, Bristol records her baptism on 19 July 1757 with a memorandum that she was born on 27 November 1756, while she herself in her memoirs gave 1758 and the day as 27 November
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Della Cruscan and newspaper verse of the 1780s and 1790s, the Romantic sonnet revival, the Gothic and domestic novel of the revolutionary decade, and the feminist prose controversy about the education and civil condition of women
literary_identity: Actress, poet, novelist, dramatist and feminist controversialist, famous first as the king's mistress 'Perdita' and afterwards as 'the English Sappho', who turned her celebrity into a professional literary career after her withdrawal from the stage
biography: Mary Darby was born in Bristol, in the winter of 1756 or 1757 by the parish register and 1758 by her own account, the daughter of Nicholas Darby, a naval captain who deserted the family, and of a mother who took in sewing and kept the household with difficulty. Fond of poetry from childhood and precociously reading her Shakespeare, she was put to work as a teacher at fourteen and, having attracted the notice of actors and writers in Bristol, was married in 1772 to Thomas Robinson, a barrister's clerk and afterwards a soldier and actor of her own family's acquaintance. She appeared on the stage at Drury Lane as Juliet in 1776 and made her lasting reputation in December 1779 as Perdita in The Winter's Tale, a performance so admired that the young Prince of Wales, afterwards George IV, paid her an assiduous court; she is generally recorded as his first public mistress, the negotiation included an offer of £20,000 to relieve her husband's debts and to settle her allowance, and the connexion ended in 1781 in a public and humiliating rupture. The birth of her daughter Maria, who became an actress and then the wife of the painter Thomas Hoppner and was widely said to be the Prince's child, did not save her marriage; she was separated from her husband, and for some years in the 1780s lived on the Continent in France and Germany, partly to remove her from scandal and partly from debt. Returning to London she recovered her position by her pen: from 1788 she wrote society and occasional verse for the newspapers, joining the fashionable Della Cruscan circle associated with Robert Merry and answering his 'Della Crusca' numbers in The World under the name of Laura, and she was celebrated as 'the English Sappho'. In the 1790s she published collected Poems (1791, with a second volume in 1793), single-issue political and occasional verse including the Monody on the late Queen of France (1793), the sonnet sequence Sappho and Phaon (1796), a volume of Lyrical Tales (1800), eight novels beginning with Vancenza (1792) and including Walsingham (1797) and The Natural Daughter (1799), three plays, and feminist prose, most confidently her Letter to the Women of England on the Injustice of Mental Subordination (1799). Like Mary Wollstonecraft she argued for the rights and education of women and was an ardent supporter of the Revolution, though her poetry also mourned its victims. Consumption, a lingering and disfiguring illness, the loss of her favour and constant money troubles marked her last years; she retired to Surrey, and died in poverty at Englefield Cottage, Englefield Green, on 26 December 1800, aged by her own register entry forty-three. Her unfinished Memoirs, written by herself, were published posthumously in 1801 in London for Richard Phillips, with simultaneous New York and later Philadelphia editions; administration of her estate was granted to her estranged husband Thomas Robinson, who in 1803 unexpectedly inherited a substantial fortune from his half-brother William.
literary_profile: Her work divides into four bodies. Her poetry, gathered from newspaper and annual verse into Poems (two volumes, the first 1791, the second 1793) and reissued as a New Edition in 1795, includes the separately printed Monody on the Queen of France (1793), sight-poems such as 'Sight, the Cavern of Woe, and Solitude' (1793) and 'Modern Manners' (1793), and the odes issued at Manchester in 1797 and 1800; its centre is Sappho and Phaon, in a Series of Legitimate Sonnets, with Other Poems, and a Ballad (1796), the self-conscious classicising of her sonnet practice and her monument of her relation with Robert Merry, and its last achievement is Lyrical Tales (1800), a volume of ballads and metrical tales which answers Wordsworth and Coleridge poem by poem. Her novels, counted as seven or eight in the surviving record, comprise Vancenza; or, The Dangers of Credulity (1792), The Widow (1794), Angelina (1796), Hubert de Sevrac (1796), Walsingham; or, The Pupil of Nature (1797), The False Friend (1799) and The Natural Daughter (1799), are epistolary and Gothic or domestic tales of credulity, seduction, concealed parentage and contested inheritance, mostly printed for herself and sold by Hookham, or issued in four volumes for Longman, and paid for at prices she had to negotiate against her declining sales. Her dramas include the opera The Lucky Escape (1778), the comedy Nobody (1794), the opera Kate of Aberdeen (withdrawn 1793) and the tragedy The Sicilian Lover (1796). Her prose of argument includes Impartial Reflections (1791), the Letter to the Women of England (1799), Thoughts on the Condition of Women (1799), a translation of the Picture of Palermo (1800) and the Memoirs of the Late Mrs. Robinson, Written by Herself (1801); her posthumous Poetical Works appeared from Richard Phillips in 1806 and again in 1824. The standard scholarly text is The Works of Mary Robinson, 8 volumes, general editor William D. Brewer (Pickering and Chatto, 2010), with Paula Byrne's biography Perdita: The Life of Mary Robinson (2004) as the usual biographical apparatus.
stylistic_characteristics: Her early verse is the ornamental, allusive manner of the Della Cruscans, which she afterwards deliberately restrained; the sonnets of Sappho and Phaon claim the 'legitimate' form against the license of contemporary experiment, with a compressed diction, an archaeological interest in Sappho's fragments and a persistent identification of the poet-lover with the ancient Lesbian. Her later lyrics and Lyrical Tales take up ballad and popular stanza, plain speech and humble speakers, and the topography of the Wye and of the revolutionary wars. The novels are written in letters or as a series of tales within a frame, mixing Gothic excitement - convents, castles, ghosts, imprisonment - with an argument about belief: Vancenza is expressly a warning against the dangers of credulity, and Walsingham turns the fashionable 'pupil of nature' into a satirised self-justifying lover. Her polemic prose is personal, indignant and closely argued, addressing women directly and using her own injuries as evidence, and the Memoirs conduct the same defence in narrative, presenting her life as a history of male seduction and female dependence. Byron's dismissal of her in English Bards and Scotch Reviewers fixed the older view of her as a decorative poet, which modern editions have overturned.
intellectual_concerns: The injustice of women's mental and civil subordination and the claims of genius and education; the double standard by which a woman's sexual history destroys her credit while making her famous; the dependence of the woman writer on subscription, patronage and the booksellers; the dangers of credulity, superstition and Gothic belief against reason and evidence; the French Revolution, its promises, its terror and its victims, mourned in the Monody on the Queen of France and celebrated elsewhere; exile, travel and the condition of the refugee; seduction, concealed parentage and the fate of the illegitimate child; and the possibility of recovering a self and a reputation in print.
historical_significance: She is one of the most published and most reviewed women poets of the 1790s and a central figure in the Romantic sonnet revival, whose Sappho and Phaon reworked the Petrarchan sequence as the record of a woman's own desire and loss, and whose Lyrical Tales (1800), printed by Longman and Rees in the same year as the second edition of Lyrical Ballads, is the most sustained contemporary poetic answer to Wordsworth and Coleridge. Her novels carried the Gothic of the 1790s into a self-conscious critique of belief and of the marriage market, and her Letter to the Women of England is a staple text of the feminist controversy of the revolutionary decade, now standard in anthologies of the period. As Perdita she became a permanent figure of the royal scandal of the Prince Regency, and her posthumous Memoirs made the actress-courtesan-author into a model of autobiographical self-defence. Recent scholarship - Brewer's eight-volume edition, Byrne's life, Ashley Cross's study of her relation to Romantic literary history and the ongoing work on the Della Cruscans - has restored her from anecdote to a writer whose career defines the possibilities and the costs of female professional authorship between 1788 and 1800.
biographical_uncertainty: Her year of birth is irreducibly uncertain: the Bristol register entry inspected by modern editors records her baptism on 19 July 1757 with a memorandum of birth on 27 November 1756, she herself gave 27 November 1758 in the Memoirs, and reference works have variously printed 1756, 1757 and 1758, while the Gentleman's Magazine obituary and some catalogues enter 1758. The terms of the Prince of Wales's settlement, including the sum of £20,000, rest on her own account and on report rather than on surviving documents; the paternity of her daughter Maria is asserted in tradition but not established; the date of her marriage to Thomas Robinson and of her separation are variously given; the number and dating of her plays and novels differ between the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry, the English Short Title Catalogue and her modern editors, and the separately printed odes of 1797 and 1800 exist in issues whose contents are not identical.
